newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FUND VIEW - Index makers confront Hong Kong dilemma.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Index makers confront Hong Kong dilemma.

text.p: ING Barings' decision not to include Hong Kong in its emerging market index ahead of the British colony's return to Chinese rule next year highlights the dilemma now faced by other index makers.

"The (gross domestic product) per capita of the combined country would qualify for membership of BEMI, but the inclusion of Hong Kong in the index would cause significant distortion," ING Barings said when it announced the decision last month.
Had it been included, Hong Kong, among the world's largest stock markets, would account for more than 30 percent of the Barings Emerging Markets Index (BEMI).
It also would have pushed out many smaller Chinese companies in favour of Hong Kong companies with index representation elsewhere, Barings said.

But the situation is certainly not straightforward. All eyes are now on Morgan Stanley Capital International and the International Finance Corp to see if they follow BEMI's lead, or cause a significant headache for chief investment officers by classifying Hong Kong as China.

"There is no easy answer," warned Bruce Johnson, ING Barings' head of index operations in London, before the decision was announced. "If you try to adopt a very pure approach in one sense, it doesn't look realistic in another sense. If you try to act against that point, rectify that, you end up with a messy rule structure. It's not easy."

Few consider Hong Kong, a well-developed commercial centre with sophisticated financial markets, an emerging market despite its incorporation into one of the world's largest developing nations on July 1 next year.

As a special administrative region with its own currency and monetary authority, Hong Kong is expected to retain its status as a global financial centre and could well gain status as the primary gateway for investment in China.
But the striking differences between the two economies helped to persuade ING Barings to exclude Hong Kong.

"(It) is expected to be governed on a substantially different basis from mainland China," ING Barings said. "Hong Kong will therefore be identifiable as a separate entity, both politically and economically."
Chief investment officers in Hong Kong acknowledged the difficulty of the decision last week.

"It's a 50-50 call on this one," said Stephen Leung, chief investment officer at BZW Asia. "There is a certain part of the market that is already well developed and pretty mature but there is another part of the market which can also be classified as emerging."
Hong Kong's eventual integration into China suggests it should be included, but initially its new status could be accommodated through the inclusion of individual stocks.

"I think a stock-picking approach could be more appropriate," Leung said. "Individual stocks, such as CITIC Pacific or even Cathay Pacific Airways, could be classified as China-related over the long term."
Ambrose Chang, chief investment officer at Daiwa International Capital Management, said Hong Kong remained too different from China for it to be included in emerging markets indices at this point.
"It depends whether you see Hong Kong as an independent financial market in Asia or as a financial market in China," he said.
Chang said he viewed Hong Kong more as an independent financial centre in Asia rather than a stock exchange in China.
